power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Emotions do not arrive as isolated labels.
They unfold, persist, subside and sometimes return, shaped by events, bodily responses and individual experience.

Yet two fields that could illuminate this movement have largely progressed separately: affective computing seeks to recognize momentary affect from physiological and behavioural signals, while affect-dynamics research studies temporal patterns using comparatively sparse self-reports.
We propose bringing them together.

Continuously inferred valencearousal trajectories, combined with information about the events that shape them, could reveal how people respond to emotional perturbations, recover and move between states.
We suggest representing intrinsic restoring tendencies through individualized, potentially multistable effective potential landscapes, while modelling event-related influences separately.
Such landscapes might eventually offer a quantitative window onto aspects of emotional temperament and regulation; their existence and interpretability are hypotheses, not assumptions.
We outline a path from controlled experiments and participant-labelled reference data to wearable sensing and personalization in daily life.
Conceptual simulations illustrate how landscapes could differ or change after experience.

Crucially, we specify how the proposal could fail: estimated landscapes must survive realistic parameter-recovery tests, comparisons with simpler dynamical models, out-of-sample prediction, and validation of the physiology-to-affect measurement chain.
If successful, this approach could connect continuous affective sensing to new questions about emotional self-awareness, resilience, relationships and mental health.
Emotional life is not a succession of independent snapshots.
A distressing event may leave one person unsettled for hours while another soon recovers; a moment of joy may fade quickly or reshape the course of a day.
To understand such differences, we need to know not only how someone feels, but how their feelings change, what sets those changes in motion and what follows when a stimulus is gone.
Affect-dynamics research already provides an important foundation.

It has described emotional variability, inertia, transitions and recovery and examined their associations with wellbeing and psychopathology (Trull et al., 2015; Wichers et al., 2015; Kuppens & Verduyn, 2017).
text.formatted: It has described emotional variability, inertia, transitions and recovery and examined their associations with wellbeing and psychopathology <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Trull et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Wichers et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Kuppens & Verduyn, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: The DynAffect model represents affect as a stochastic process attracted toward a person-specific home base (Kuppens et al., 2010; Oravecz et al., 2011).
text.formatted: The DynAffect model represents affect as a stochastic process attracted toward a person-specific home base <ref type="bibr">(Kuppens et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Oravecz et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Work on state-space grids, complex systems and multistable affect has further explored attractors and transitions (Hollenstein, 2007 (Hollenstein, , 2015;; van de Leemput et al., 2014; Loossens et al., 2020; Olthof et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Work on state-space grids, complex systems and multistable affect has further explored attractors and transitions <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Hollenstein, 2007</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Hollenstein, , 2015;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">van de Leemput et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Loossens et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Olthof et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: More recently, individual stability landscapes have been inferred from momentary valence data (Goicoechea et al., 2025).
text.formatted: More recently, individual stability landscapes have been inferred from momentary valence data <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Goicoechea et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: These advances also show why the problem remains open.
Most empirical studies sample affect a few times a day, often without detailed records of the events that occurred between reports.

Apparently distinct emotional states might reflect multiple internal attractors, changing situations or properties of the rating scale rather than the same mechanism (Haslbeck et al., 2023; Haqiqatkhah et al., 2024; Ryan et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Apparently distinct emotional states might reflect multiple internal attractors, changing situations or properties of the rating scale rather than the same mechanism <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Haslbeck et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Haqiqatkhah et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Ryan et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Dense observations alone will not resolve this ambiguity; we also need information about the forces acting on the person.
Affective computing offers a complementary possibility.
Wearable and other physiological sensors can provide much denser observations, and emotion recognition has made substantial technical progress (Shu et al., 2018; Saganowski et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Wearable and other physiological sensors can provide much denser observations, and emotion recognition has made substantial technical progress <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Shu et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Saganowski et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Yet many systems remain trained on short laboratory recordings and evaluated on momentary categories or ratings, not on the course of an emotional episode (Larradet et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Yet many systems remain trained on short laboratory recordings and evaluated on momentary categories or ratings, not on the course of an emotional episode <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Larradet et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Continuous monitoring outside the laboratory is increasingly feasible, although its interpretation remains difficult (Saganowski, 2022; Gutierrez Maestro et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Continuous monitoring outside the laboratory is increasingly feasible, although its interpretation remains difficult <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Saganowski, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Gutierrez Maestro et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Our proposal is to connect these approaches.
Physiological measurements could support continuous estimates of valence and arousal, while records of meaningful events and their appraisal provide context for those trajectories.
Repeated departures from and returns toward familiar emotional regions could then be used to investigate person-specific response and restoring dynamics.
We illustrate one possible mathematical representation-a malleable effective potential landscape-not as an established map of temperament, but as a testable hypothesis.
The framework moves from measurement (Sections 2-3) to dynamical modelling (Section 4), empirical tests (Section 5), research opportunities (Section 6) and ethical safeguards (Section 7).
Automatic emotion recognition (AER) should not be understood as reading a person's inner life directly from a sensor.

Emotion involves external and internal events, appraisal, bodily change and conscious experience, and different theories place different emphasis on those components (Scherer, 2009; Kuppens & Tong, 2010; Barrett, 2017).
text.formatted: Emotion involves external and internal events, appraisal, bodily change and conscious experience, and different theories place different emphasis on those components <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Scherer, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Kuppens & Tong, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Barrett, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Figure 1 illustrates the view that motivates our proposal.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref> illustrates the view that motivates our proposal.

text.text: Physiological activity-including cardiovascular, electrodermal and other bodily responses-both accompanies emotional processing and contributes to the sensations through which feelings become meaningful (Purves et al., 2001; Khalsa et al., 2018; Carvalho & Damasio, 2021).
text.formatted: Physiological activity-including cardiovascular, electrodermal and other bodily responses-both accompanies emotional processing and contributes to the sensations through which feelings become meaningful <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Purves et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Khalsa et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Carvalho & Damasio, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: The same bodily pattern can nevertheless be experienced differently depending on the person and context (Moors, 2017).
text.formatted: The same bodily pattern can nevertheless be experienced differently depending on the person and context <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Moors, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: A physiology-based model, f(x), therefore learns an imperfect relationship between measured signals and reported affect, not a universal correspondence between body and emotion.
That relationship may change across people, contexts and time; individualized calibration can improve performance in some settings (Han et al., 2024; Li & Washington, 2024).
text.formatted: That relationship may change across people, contexts and time; individualized calibration can improve performance in some settings <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Han et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Li & Washington, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Even an accurate estimate of how someone feels at one instant, however, cannot explain why they arrived there or where they will go next.
That is the missing temporal question (Trull et al., 2015).
text.formatted: That is the missing temporal question <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Trull et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Figure 2 outlines the transition we envisage: from isolated emotion classification to continuous, personally calibrated affect estimation in daily life.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref> outlines the transition we envisage: from isolated emotion classification to continuous, personally calibrated affect estimation in daily life.

text.text: It also places events alongside affective trajectories.
Without knowing what happened, a long negative episode could reflect strong reactivity, repeated adversity or slow recovery-very different accounts of the same observations.

Controlled elicitation studies have enabled progress in physiological affect recognition, but they often use sparse labels and test generalization only within laboratory conditions (Saganowski, 2022; Larradet et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Controlled elicitation studies have enabled progress in physiological affect recognition, but they often use sparse labels and test generalization only within laboratory conditions <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Saganowski, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Larradet et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Some research now demonstrates the value of personalized models (Han et al., 2024; Li & Washington, 2024).
text.formatted: Some research now demonstrates the value of personalized models <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Han et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Li & Washington, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: A next step is to design studies expressly for tracking change, rather than merely assigning a label to each clip.
We envision first training a population-level model, f(x)g, in a diverse sample with synchronized physiological recordings and continuous or near-continuous reports of valence and arousal.
Existing datasets demonstrate that such annotation is feasible (Sharma et al., 2019; Sharma et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Existing datasets demonstrate that such annotation is feasible <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Sharma et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Sharma et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Crucially, stimulus onset and offset, pre-stimulus reference periods and post-stimulus recovery should all be recorded.
Repeated exposures across emotional directions and intensities would help distinguish response sensitivity from subsequent recovery.
There is no perfect way to obtain a continuous record of subjective feeling.
Participants can rate affect as it unfolds, but doing so may change the experience.
Alternatively, they can revisit a recording and reconstruct what they felt, as in the affect-rating-dial tradition (Gottman & Levenson, 1985; Ruef & Levenson, 2007).
text.formatted: Alternatively, they can revisit a recording and reconstruct what they felt, as in the affect-rating-dial tradition <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Gottman & Levenson, 1985;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Ruef & Levenson, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: This reduces interference during the original episode but adds memory, habituation and timing errors.

Because simultaneous continuous ratings have also proved feasible (Sharma et al., 2019), the two approaches should be compared empirically, rather than either being treated as unproblematic ground truth.
text.formatted: Because simultaneous continuous ratings have also proved feasible <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Sharma et al., 2019)</ref>, the two approaches should be compared empirically, rather than either being treated as unproblematic ground truth.

text.text: A population model trained in the laboratory will still face unfamiliar people and situations.

We therefore envisage a second stage in which wearable sensing and a smartphone app provide provisional affect estimates during ordinary activities, while users occasionally report their experience and relevant events.
Earlier work has already combined mobile sensing with self-reported affect and has explored wearable monitoring outside the laboratory (Asselbergs et al., 2016; Gutierrez Maestro et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Earlier work has already combined mobile sensing with self-reported affect and has explored wearable monitoring outside the laboratory <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Asselbergs et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Gutierrez Maestro et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Prompts could appear when affect seems to change or predictions are uncertain, supplemented by randomly timed prompts to avoid sampling only detected episodes.
The resulting reports could improve the shared model and calibrate it to the individual, yielding f(x)i.
Once a robust individualized f(x)i model is developed, it would replace the population-level f(x)g model as the automatic emotion recognition model for the user.
Prompt probabilities, missing reports and model updates must be documented: changes in an algorithm should never be mistaken for changes in a person's emotional life.
Pilot studies should establish whether such monitoring is accurate, tolerable and useful before wider deployment.

We anticipate that, the higher the difference between the individual user and the population used to train f(x)g for relevant factors (such as, for example, sex, age, ethnicity, socioeconomic status etc..), more data will be necessary to develop a robust f(x)i.
A wearable device might record photoplethysmography, electrodermal activity, movement and skin temperature.
A phone could translate these signals into uncertain estimates of affect that are reviewed later, rather than demanding constant attention (Figure 3).

text.text: A user might see how feelings changed over a day, which events preceded a lasting shift, or how quickly they tended to recover.
With further validation, these records could support self-awareness, reflection on triggers, personalized coping, conversations with loved ones or psychotherapy.
Their purpose should be to support introspection, not replace it.
Estimates should be presented with uncertainty, and users should remain free to disagree with them.

Affect dynamics already includes summary indices and formal time-series models, including autoregressive and stochastic approaches to person-specific restoring tendencies (Lodewyckx et al., 2011; Hamaker et al., 2015; Kuppens et al., 2010; Oravecz et al., 2011).

text.text: Our specific proposal is to use densely sampled, physiologyinformed valence-arousal trajectories to estimate restoring dynamics, while separately accounting for measured events.
The distinction matters because spending a long time in one affective region does not, by itself, establish that the region is an intrinsic attractor.
Repeated perturbations and recovery periods may provide more informative evidence than occupancy alone.
Imagine an individual's emotional state moving across a landscape.
Valleys represent regions toward which the state tends to return; ridges make some transitions less likely; and a change in the landscape alters what is stable.
We formalize this intuition with an effective potential U(x, y) over valence and arousal.
Its negative gradient describes the restoring tendency in a gradient-driven model.
Local minima correspond to attractors, although whether human affect actually obeys such dynamics remains an empirical question.
If supported, landscape geometry may offer a way to describe aspects of emotional regulation and temperament.

DynAffect offers a useful point of departure: its personspecific home base and restoring strength correspond, in a simplified first-order formulation, to a single quadratic well (Kuppens et al., 2010; Oravecz et al., 2011).

text.text: Our hypothesis permits more than one basin.
We also use inertia in the illustrations to depict overshoot and settling, but do not assume that inertia is necessary or identifiable in real affective data.
The first-order model is our proposed starting point for estimation.
Let X(t) denote a person's position in valence-arousal space.

Here -∇U is the proposed restoring tendency, T(t) represents event-related influences, and dW(t) captures stochastic variation.
For Figure 4, we extend this simple model to allow inertia and use transient event forces and a potential composed of basins and elevated regions (Supplementary Methods).

text.text: Crucially, the affective force of an event is not fixed: it depends on appraisal, sensitivity and context.
The challenge for empirical work is to separate these external influences from any intrinsic restoring dynamics.
In the baseline simulation (Figure 4, left), a relatively calm region coexists with a secondary, high-arousal negative-valence attractor.

text.text: A distressing event temporarily displaces the system into the latter; a calming event helps it return; and a positive surprise produces a shorter excursion.
The same imposed events could have very different consequences in another landscape.
The other panels imagine how that landscape might change with experience.
In the middle panel, a stronger central attractor and disappearance of the distressed basin make prolonged negative episodes less likely.
But a uniformly stronger attractor also reduces movement toward positive states: resilience and emotional flexibility are not necessarily the same thing.
In the right panel, a weakened central basin and deeper distressed attractor make recovery from an adverse event more difficult.
These are hypotheses about possible patterns of change, not simulations of psychotherapy or trauma outcomes.
Figure 4 therefore expresses a possibility, not evidence that such landscapes exist in people.

text.text: It is a way of asking whether persistent distress reflects a stable attractor, a prolonged response to events, or some combination-and what observations would distinguish these accounts.
The imposed event forces are held fixed only to isolate the geometry in the illustration; in real life, appraisal and event sensitivity can change as well.
The idea should be judged by what it predicts, not by how intuitive its visualizations appear.
A credible landscape must be recoverable from realistic measurements, outperform simpler explanations and describe something reproducible about a person.
Our preliminary simulations are a limited numerical check, not a validation of the framework.
The first test is parameter recovery.

Starting with simulated trajectories whose landscape and event inputs are known, we should vary sampling density, sensor-derived measurement error, delay, session duration and the number and type of perturbations.
We can then ask which aspects of the landscape can be recovered.

Experience-sampling work suggests caution: even simple affect-dynamics summaries can require substantial observation, and nonlinear models may need long series to earn their complexity (Pirla et al., 2023; Cui et al., 2026).

text.text: Dense wearable recordings do not automatically provide dense *information* about emotion.
Repeated, well-characterized event responses may be particularly valuable for identifying restoring tendencies (Oravecz et al., 2011; Friedrich et al., 2011).

text.text: This is a proof of numerical feasibility under favorable conditions, not evidence of general identifiability.
It leaves open the harder problem of simultaneously discovering landscape structure and unknown event inputs, and it does not establish validity for real emotional data.
A multi-basin model should be adopted only if it explains or predicts trajectories better than credible simpler models.

These include a single attractor, as in DynAffect; switching situations that elicit different affective states without intrinsic multistability (Ryan et al., 2025; Hamaker & Grasman, 2012); and a single attractor whose location drifts with context or time (Bringmann et al., 2017).

text.text: Tests should predict heldout responses and recovery periods, keep each episode intact across validation splits, and allow each candidate the same event information.
Attractive plots or in-sample fit are not enough.
Claims about temperament require additional evidence.
Person-specific features should show meaningful reliability across independent sessions and predict subsequent responses better than population-level models.
If landscape features change substantially from week to week without major events, they may describe circumstances rather than dispositions.

They must also add information beyond simpler summaries such as mean affect and variability, which already explain much of what affect-dynamics metrics predict about wellbeing (Dejonckheere et al., 2019).
text.formatted: They must also add information beyond simpler summaries such as mean affect and variability, which already explain much of what affect-dynamics metrics predict about wellbeing <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Dejonckheere et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Malleability is compatible with reliability, but only if the expected timescales of stability and change are specified and tested.
Most importantly, the emotional trajectories would themselves be estimates.
Physiological responses lag, and recognition models smooth, filter and shrink predictions toward familiar values.
These procedures can create apparent inertia, restoring forces and boundaries even when they do not exist in the underlying experience.
Self-report brings its own delays and scale effects (Haslbeck et al., 2023; Haqiqatkhah et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Self-report brings its own delays and scale effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Haslbeck et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Haqiqatkhah et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Validation should therefore compare physiology-inferred trajectories with high-resolution participant reports, propagate uncertainty into the dynamical model, and examine generalization across people, elicitors and contexts (Sharma et al., 2019; Dollack et al., 2023).

text.text: Physical activity, posture, sleep and other physiological influences must also be considered.
A convincing finding cannot be an artefact of the affectrecognition algorithm.
Finally, timescale matters.

Laboratory episodes lasting minutes may tell us about local recovery near a familiar state; establishing multiple attractors, their persistence and their possible plasticity would require much longer naturalistic observations, ideally across days or weeks.
If the proposed measurement and modelling pipeline proves reliable, it could open several research directions that are difficult to pursue with occasional affect reports alone (Figure 5).

text.text: Individual differences in appraisal and reactivity.
People can experience the same event differently, or interpret similar bodily responses in different ways.

Pairing personalized affect estimators with measured events could help separate differences in expressed or physiological reactions from differences in reported experience, although a simple exchange of models between individuals would not, by itself, identify appraisal.
Controlled comparisons and explicit measurement models would be needed.
Social and interpersonal dynamics.
Synchronized trajectories from partners, families or other close relationships could illuminate emotional co-regulation, lagged responses and social synchrony (Mayo & Gordon, 2020).
text.formatted: Synchronized trajectories from partners, families or other close relationships could illuminate emotional co-regulation, lagged responses and social synchrony <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Mayo & Gordon, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Does another person's presence change the speed of recovery, the likelihood of transition or the apparent stability of an affective region?
Such questions require dyadic designs that distinguish shared events from genuine interpersonal influence.
Development over the lifespan.
Repeated measurements could investigate whether patterns of emotional responsiveness and recovery change with age or major life experiences (Wrzus et al., 2014; Bleidorn et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Repeated measurements could investigate whether patterns of emotional responsiveness and recovery change with age or major life experiences <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Wrzus et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Bleidorn et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: If landscapes are identifiable, their evolving geometry could offer a new description of those changes.
Temperament and its determinants.

Reliable person-specific features-such as restoring strength, transition propensity or barrier geometry-could be studied alongside established measures of temperament and personality, and eventually in genetic and environmental research (Rothbart et al., 2000; Kandler & Instinske, 2025).

text.text: Their value would depend on being stable, interpretable and informative beyond conventional affect summaries.
Emotion-focused psychotherapy, meditation or other interventions might change not only average distress but also the ease of leaving or recovering from difficult states.

The landscape representation offers testable hypotheses about such changes, provided treatment effects on event exposure and appraisal are distinguished from changes in restoring dynamics (Hayes & Andrews, 2020; Olthof et al., 2023).
text.formatted: The landscape representation offers testable hypotheses about such changes, provided treatment effects on event exposure and appraisal are distinguished from changes in restoring dynamics <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Hayes & Andrews, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Olthof et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: More broadly, this approach could connect the technological ability to observe affect more frequently with the scientific ambition to understand emotional change-without assuming in advance that landscapes are the right model.
A system that continuously estimates a person's emotions would be more than a scientific instrument.
It could alter how someone interprets themselves and how others treat them.

Four concerns deserve attention from the start: the psychological effects of monitoring, privacy and governance, overconfidence in model outputs, and unequal performance (Martinez-Martin et al., 2018; Martinez-Martin et al., 2021).

text.text: Effects of monitoring.
Tracking affect may support reflection, but may also intensify rumination or dependence on an app.
A graphic labelled as a person's "distressed basin" could be mistaken for an immutable identity rather than a contingent model estimate.
These effects should be evaluated prospectively, not assumed beneficial (Faurholt-Jepsen et al., 2019).
text.formatted: These effects should be evaluated prospectively, not assumed beneficial <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Faurholt-Jepsen et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Privacy and governance.
Emotion-related recordings can expose intimate information about health, relationships and behavior.
People must retain meaningful control over collection, access and deletion, and there should be strong protections against unwanted use by employers, educational institutions and insurers.

Existing legal restrictions, including the European Union's Artificial Intelligence Act, reinforce the importance of context-specific safeguards (European Parliament and Council of the European Union, 2024).
Reification.
A predicted trajectory is not a direct measurement of inner experience.
Clinicians, partners or users themselves may give an appealing visualization more authority than it warrants.
Estimates should display uncertainty and permit correction or disagreement, in keeping with critiques of overconfident emotion recognition (Cross et al., 2023; Rad et al., 2025).

text.text: Unequal performance.
Models may work less well for particular ages, cultural backgrounds or physiological profiles, creating unequal benefits and potential harms.
Performance disparities, including those arising from sensor measurement, require direct evaluation rather than assurances of generalizability (Cross et al., 2023; O'Leary et al., 2024).

Velocities are estimated from the observed positions by finite differences.

For each interior time step the model predicts the next velocity from the current velocity, the damping, the gradient of the candidate landscape at the current position and the trigger force at the current time; under the model the residual between observed and predicted next velocity is Gaussian noise with variance σₚ²dt in each dimension.
The negative log-likelihood is the sum over steps and dimensions of the squared residuals scaled by that variance, plus the log-determinant term that ties σₚ to the residual scale.
Steps at which the trajectory touches the boundary of the valence-arousal square are excluded.
Quiescent stretches inform estimation of the landscape, damping and noise.

The first step after an onset provides information about the net push through its contribution pⱼdt to the expected velocity increment, in addition to landscape, damping and any remaining event forces.
Subsequent relaxation provides information about λⱼ jointly with restoring dynamics and damping.
The continuous parameters were estimated by minimizing the negative log-likelihood with the L-BFGS-B quasi-Newton algorithm (SciPy) using forward-difference gradients.

Basin centres were initialized at the peaks of a kernel density estimate of the trajectory, hill centres at high-arousal, neutral-valence positions with random jitter, and other parameters at mid-range defaults; five random restarts were run per configuration and the fit with the lowest negative log-likelihood retained.

In Regime C the number of basins and hills was selected by an outer search over N_b ∈ {1, …, 4} and N_h ∈ {0, 1, 2}, scoring each configuration by the Bayesian information criterion, BIC = 2•NLL + k•log(n), with k = 5N_b + 5N_h + 8 free parameters and n the number of interior residuals.
In Regime B the overdamped reduction of the model was used, because acceleration cannot be estimated from widely spaced samples.
When nothing about the triggers is given, four steps surround the joint fit.

First, candidate onsets are detected as change points in the magnitude of successive velocity differences, computed from the finite-difference velocity: a step is flagged when it exceeds a robust threshold, the median plus 4 × 1.4826 × the median absolute deviation, so that the event spikes themselves do not inflate the threshold; flagged steps closer than 15 time units are merged into one event, because an underdamped kick rings for several steps; the first flagged step of each cluster is taken as the onset; and the first 5 time units are skipped to avoid the start-up transient.
Second, each detected trigger's push vector is warm-started from the velocity jump at its onset after subtracting a damping-only prediction, and its decay from a default of 5 time units.
Third, landscape, damping, noise and all (pⱼ, λⱼ) are fitted jointly with onsets fixed at the detected times.

Fourth, residuals under the fitted model are recomputed with 10 time units masked around each known onset, the change-point rule is rerun on them to catch weak events that the first pass missed, and any new event is added and the model refitted, for up to three passes.

Finally, because the detector can over-detect, candidates are ranked by recovered push magnitude and nested subsets (all candidates, drop the weakest, drop the two weakest, and so on) are refitted and scored by BIC with k = 5N_b + 5N_h + 8 + 3N_triggers; the subset with the lowest BIC is retained.
A detected change point is a candidate disturbance in the simulated dynamics, not independent verification of a real-world event or its psychological meaning.
Independently recorded events and appraisal reports would be needed to establish that interpretation in human data.

Coverage limits.
Hill and confinement parameters are weakly recovered in several fits, and some secondary-basin parameters are also inaccurate in the structure-selection run (Figure S1).

text.text: Poorly visited regions provide limited information, but a single fit cannot separate this explanation from parameter trade-offs, optimization error or discretization effects.
Recovery of basin geometry and event parameters must therefore be assessed separately, with replicated simulations and uncertainty estimates rather than a blanket claim of accurate recovery.

The checks provide conditional evidence of numerical recovery for selected landscape and event features in one simulated trajectory; they do not establish general structural or practical identifiability.
Their scope is bounded in five ways.

They concern one simulated person with three sharp, well-separated, exponentially decaying events; overlapping events, ramped onsets and sustained stimuli, which are not represented by the instantaneous-onset exponential forces tested here, have not been tested.

The noise level is low relative to the event kicks (spikes 5-15 times the detection threshold) and to what physiology-inferred trajectories will carry; the residual re-detection and BIC steps exist for noisier cases but have not been stress-tested.

Onsets are fixed at the detected step rather than refined continuously, which introduces onset uncertainty up to the sampling resolution and may become more consequential under sparse or noisy observation.
The landscape family used for fitting is the family that generated the data, so misspecification is not tested.
Finally, U is identifiable only up to an additive constant, and its numerical scale depends on the affect coordinates, time units and first-or second-order convention.
Occupancy alone identifies a potential relative to noise; drift-based fitting with known time units can estimate restoring coefficients and noise separately under the stated model assumptions.

Ethical considerations, potential harms and mitigation strategiesThe possibility that a person's emotional life has a discernible dynamic structure is both scientifically compelling and personally meaningful.
Affect-dynamics research has supplied models of temporal change; affective computing offers increasingly dense observations.
Together, they may allow us to ask not only how someone feels, but what moves them, what helps them recover and what patterns persist.
We have proposed individualized effective potential landscapes as one way to express-and test-those questions, not as a literal map of the mind.

Existing work on attractors and affect dynamics provides the foundation; the proposed advance lies in linking continuous physiology-informed trajectories with measured events and investigating whether restoring forces and multistability can be identified in individual lives.
The simulations show what the model can express, not what human emotion necessarily does.
Rigorous measurement validation, recovery studies and comparisons with simpler explanations will determine whether the landscape hypothesis survives.
Even if it does not, the effort to connect dense, personally meaningful affect measurements with models of emotional change could advance the study of emotion, relationships and mental health.
